name: Low-carb diet

lead: A low-carb diet cuts bread, sugar, pasta and starches and relies more on meat, fish, eggs, dairy, nuts and non-starchy vegetables. People use it to lose body fat, sharpen their physique and, some say, clear their skin. It is often positioned between ordinary eating and stricter carnivore regimens.

There is no single definition: one professional body treats under 20 percent of energy from carbohydrate as low-carb, another uses under 25 percent, and ketogenic versions go below about 50 grams a day. Trials generally find slightly more weight loss than low-fat diets in the short and medium term, with the gap shrinking over time, and long-term results track calorie intake and adherence. Higher protein may increase fullness. Forum users disagree, with some reporting hunger, low energy and weaker gym performance while others tolerate it well.

paras: People swap starches for protein, fats and vegetables, often with higher protein to help keep muscle while cutting. Early loss is partly water, and fat loss follows over weeks to months. Many use a moderate version rather than ketogenic levels.

Reported side effects include constipation, headache, bad breath, cramps and weakness. Long-term cohort data are mixed, and cardiology and dietetic bodies advise discussing very low-carb versions with a clinician. Ketoacidosis is rare but documented, mostly in diabetes.

chain: Lower calorie intake, less water weight
angle.text: Users cut carbohydrates to lower calorie intake and body fat for a leaner physique, sometimes pairing it with high protein to keep muscle. Trials show slightly faster early weight loss than low-fat diets, with the gap narrowing over time.

lead: A low-carbohydrate diet restricts carbohydrate relative to typical Western eating, cutting sugars, bread, pasta and starches and leaning more on meat, fish, eggs, dairy, nuts and non-starchy vegetables. There is no standard definition: one professional body treats under 20 percent of energy from carbohydrate as low-carb, another uses under 25 percent, and ketogenic variants typically go below about 50 grams a day, which makes studies hard to compare [1].

People use it to look leaner. The chain people describe runs from lower carbohydrate intake and higher protein, to less hunger and fewer calories eaten, to loss of body fat and water, to a more defined jawline, cheek and midsection; some also report clearer skin and less bloating. Early scale drops are partly water, which is lost along with stored glycogen [1][2]. In looksmaxxing communities it sits between ordinary eating and stricter carnivore regimens, and forum users hold opposing views, with some reporting hunger, fatigue and poor training on it [2].

Published research generally finds that low-carb diets produce slightly more weight loss than low-fat diets in the short and medium term, with the difference small and shrinking over time; in the 609-person DIETFITS trial, 12-month losses were 6.0 kg on a low-carbohydrate diet and 5.3 kg on a low-fat diet, a difference that was not statistically significant [1][3]. Major health bodies differ in how they position the approach, and the diet has a long history, from nineteenth-century diabetes care and William Banting's 1863 booklet to the Atkins boom of the late twentieth century [1].

paras: Low-carb diets replace refined and starchy carbohydrate with foods higher in protein and fat. Non-starchy vegetables are usually retained.[1] Intensity ranges from mild reduction (around 40 percent of energy from carbohydrate in one 2016 classification) to very low intakes of about 50 grams a day, and the modified Atkins pattern can be under 10 grams a day.[1]

Popular named plans such as the Zone and South Beach diets are sometimes marketed as low-carb but have been described as closer to moderate carbohydrate intake.[1] Ketogenic diets and carnivore-style diets sit at the stricter end of the spectrum.

Wikipedia notes that research suggests carbohydrate quality matters more than quantity, with high-fibre slowly digested carbohydrate seen as healthier than refined sugary forms [1]. Variants discussed in appearance and fitness circles include ketogenic eating, in which the liver makes ketone bodies as fuel when carbohydrate is very low; modified Atkins; the very-low-calorie ketogenic diet, capped around 800 kilocalories a day under medical supervision; and the all-animal carnivore diet [1][4].

Leanness. Reducing body fat is the main appearance goal people give for cutting carbohydrate. Proponents say removing sugary and starchy foods lowers appetite and makes a calorie deficit easier to hold, and that higher protein helps keep them full while preserving muscle during a cut; a 2012 review supports protein's role in satiety and in sparing fat-free mass during weight loss [5]. The first week or two of a low-carb diet usually includes water loss, which the Atkins article notes is a large part of early scale changes [6].

Skin. A looksmaxxing rationale is that fewer high-glycaemic foods means less insulin signalling and therefore less acne. A 2022 systematic review of diet and acne (34 articles) reported that high glycaemic index and glycaemic load were associated with acne occurrence and severity, supported by randomised trials, with the authors describing the effect as modest [3]. That review addresses glycaemic load generally rather than low-carb diets as a named pattern.

Training and energy. Gym-focused users weigh appearance against performance. A three-week crossover trial in 24 active adults found peak power and time to exhaustion were higher after a high-carbohydrate low-fat diet than after a low-carbohydrate diet, while both diets reduced body mass and fat mass and neither significantly changed lean mass [7].

In 1797 the British surgeon John Rollo treated diabetic army officers with a low-carbohydrate regimen, and very low-carbohydrate eating was a standard diabetes treatment through the nineteenth century [1]. Jean Anthelme Brillat-Savarin promoted a low-carbohydrate approach in The Physiology of Taste in 1825 [1]. In 1863 William Banting, an English undertaker, published a letter describing his weight loss after cutting bread, butter, milk, sugar, beer and potatoes; the word banting entered popular use for dieting [1].

The related ketogenic diet was developed in the 1920s as an epilepsy therapy: Russell Wilder coined the term and first tested it in 1921, and by 1925 a report found 60 percent of 37 young patients seizure-free; anticonvulsant drugs pushed it into a last-resort role until Jim Abrahams publicised it in 1994 after it controlled his son's epilepsy [4]. In the 1960s further low-carb plans appeared, including the Air Force diet and the Drinking Man's Diet, and in 1981 David Jenkins introduced the glycemic index [1].

Robert Atkins published Dr. Atkins' Diet Revolution in 1972, an approach Wikipedia says was inspired by Alfred Pennington's work at DuPont during the Second World War; mainstream medical bodies criticised it [1][6]. Atkins Nutritionals was founded in 1989; popularity peaked in 2003 and 2004, when about one in eleven North American adults said they followed a low-carb diet, and the company filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection on 31 July 2005 [6]. Atkins died in 2003, and a 2004 lawsuit blaming the diet for a customer's raised cholesterol was dismissed in 2007 on First Amendment grounds [6]. Some estimates put the peak share of Americans on such diets as high as 18 percent [1].

Reviews report that low-carb diets often lead to slightly greater weight loss than low-fat diets in the short and medium term, an advantage described as small and equivalent to roughly 100 kilocalories a day that fades over time.[1] A 2022 Cochrane review found no benefit over balanced diets at two years.[1]

The carbohydrate-insulin hypothesis, promoted by Gary Taubes and David Ludwig, predicted a large metabolic advantage for low-carb eating; a well-funded test did not confirm this, and researcher Kevin Hall concluded the hypothesis had been falsified by that experiment, according to the Wikipedia summary.[1] Proponents of the hypothesis continue to dispute such interpretations.
Protein, which tends to rise on low-carb diets, has been reviewed as supporting satiety, preservation of fat-free mass and maintenance of energy expenditure during weight loss.[5]

A 2024 network meta-analysis of seven randomised trials (1,004 participants) found that all of the diets compared produced weight loss, with the low-carbohydrate diet showing smaller loss than the Mediterranean diet in direct comparison [8].

In type 2 diabetes, carbohydrate restriction often improves blood glucose control, though weight loss is not consistently better, and some guidance accepts reduced-carbohydrate options for people who cannot reach glucose targets.[1] A small study found that carbohydrate restriction combined with walking after meals reduced post-meal glucose spikes and improved endothelial function in type 2 diabetes.[9]

For liver fat, a comparison of low-fat and low-carb interventions found that common liver fat scores tracked changes in liver fat under a low-fat diet but not under a low-carb diet.[10] A review of dietary strategies for fatty liver disease discusses carbohydrate restriction among several approaches.[11]

Ketogenic diets, the strictest form, have been reviewed as a possible therapy for mood disorders, with the authors describing the evidence base as developing,[12] and a pilot experience reported possible benefit in refractory migraine.[13]

Commonly reported effects include constipation, headache, bad breath, muscle cramps and weakness.[1] Ketosis is a normal metabolic state, but ketoacidosis, a rare and potentially life-threatening condition, has been reported in case reports with Atkins and South Beach diets.[1] Very restrictive versions risk fibre and micronutrient shortfalls, and rare case reports describe thiamine-deficiency encephalopathy, optic neuropathy and other complications.[1]

Cohort evidence on long-term use is mixed. Diets followed for under two years did not worsen cardiovascular markers in reviews cited by Wikipedia, whereas long-term adherence has been associated with higher total and LDL cholesterol, and one study linked it to higher cardiovascular mortality.[1] A large Japanese cohort associated high adherence with higher overall cancer risk, attributed mainly to animal rather than plant sources of fat.[1]
Low-carb diets may reduce capacity for high-intensity exercise and slow muscle glycogen recovery.[1]

Specific to ketogenic eating, Wikipedia's epilepsy-therapy summary lists constipation and, in children on the strict medical version, slowed growth, bone problems and kidney stones, plus raised blood lipids; the weight-loss versions are less restrictive [4]. The Atkins article records the dismissal of a 2004 lawsuit over cholesterol and a 2005 company bankruptcy, and cites criticism of the diet by medical associations as nutritionally unbalanced because of its saturated fat [6].

The US National Academy of Medicine sets an average recommended intake of 130 grams of carbohydrate a day, and the FAO and WHO recommend that most dietary energy come from carbohydrate.[1] The UK NHS describes carbohydrate as the body's main energy source.[1]

The American College of Cardiology advises discussion with a clinician before very low-carb diets and notes possible long-term LDL increases; the American Heart Association (2021) found insufficient evidence that ketogenic diets promote heart health; and the American Diabetes Association treats reduced-carb eating as one viable approach for some people with type 2 diabetes.[1] The British Dietetic Association listed the ketogenic diet among its worst celebrity diets in 2018.[1]

The 2015-2020 US Dietary Guidelines did not endorse low-carbohydrate diets, and Wikipedia reports that the carbohydrate-insulin hypothesis promoted by Gary Taubes and David Ludwig is considered poorly supported by most researchers, while its proponents dispute that assessment [1]. A 2021 umbrella review in type 2 diabetes found no weight-loss advantage over other diets, and one study found low-carb dieters had the most lapses and dropouts by two years [1].

Many randomised trials and meta-analyses of low-carb diets exist, mainly for weight loss, diabetes and epilepsy. Wikipedia notes that many lower-quality meta-analyses favoured low-carb diets, a pattern that may reflect publication bias, while higher-quality reviews show little difference [1]. No trial has studied low-carb diets specifically for facial appearance or attractiveness.

DIETFITS (JAMA 2018) randomised 609 overweight adults to a healthy low-fat or healthy low-carbohydrate diet for 12 months; weight change was -5.3 kg and -6.0 kg, a 0.7 kg difference that was not significant, and neither genotype pattern nor insulin secretion predicted which diet suited an individual better [3]. A 2015 inpatient crossover study by Kevin Hall and colleagues at the NIH, in 19 adults with obesity, held calories equal for six days: body fat loss was about 53 g a day on carbohydrate restriction and 89 g a day on fat restriction, a difference the authors reported as significant over the short term, while predicting the body would minimise such differences over longer periods [3]. This study is part of the evidence debated in relation to the carbohydrate-insulin hypothesis, which proponents continue to defend [1].

Small studies cover related questions, including carbohydrate restriction in women with breast cancer, which reported improvements in quality of life and body composition [14], and a mouse study of a low-carbohydrate, high-protein diet in prostate tumours [15].

On looksmax.org, discussions about carbohydrates sit alongside carnivore and animal-based diet threads. One widely replied thread argues against low-carb eating, with its author describing constant hunger, low energy, poor mood and low libido after one to two months of very low carbohydrate intake despite eating eggs, liver and chicken, and recommending lower-glycaemic carbohydrate sources instead.[2] Other users report fat loss and appetite control on reduced-carbohydrate diets in related threads.

The thread's replies split the debate in a familiar way: some posters say any carbohydrate is fine if it is low glycaemic, while others in the same community advocate carnivore eating; the thread's author names carnivore advocates as the group he is arguing against [2]. On T Nation, training logs and diet threads discuss carbohydrate intake for lifters, including a linked T Nation article titled on carb intake for natural lifters, which argues that very low-carb diets reduce muscle gains [16].

lore.intro: Low-carb eating is discussed on looksmax.org both as a leanness tool and as a diet some users say left them depleted.[2]
